title: Trump Administration Moves to Rescind Roadless Rule Protecting 59 Million Forest Acres
excerpt: The proposed rule would lift a 25-year-old ban on logging, roads and mining in undeveloped national forests, shifting authority to local managers amid record wildfire season.
body:
• The U.S. Forest Service filed a proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule, which protects nearly 59 million acres of undeveloped national forest from road-building, logging and mining.
  • Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins called the rule "absurd" and said rescinding it would improve forest health, while environmental groups warn it will increase wildfire risk and threaten clean water supplies.
  • The Big Beautiful Bill mandates a 250 million board-feet annual increase in timber sales through 2034, roughly an 8% yearly jump from 2023 levels.
  • The public comment period on the proposed rule runs until September 21, with a final decision expected in late 2026.

The Trump administration on Tuesday filed a formal proposal to rescind the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, a 25-year-old regulation that bans logging, road construction and mining across nearly 59 million acres of undeveloped national forest land — roughly 30% of the entire National Forest System, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

The proposed rule would shift decision-making authority to local forest managers, a move Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins framed as restoring common-sense management. "Today, we filed a proposal to restore authority to local forest managers who know the land best, removing the barriers that have kept them from doing the work the land demands," Rollins said in a statement.

A Rule Born in the Clinton Era

The Roadless Rule was enacted in the final weeks of the Clinton administration in 2001, designed to protect endangered species and 350 watersheds within national forests used for drinking water from Alaska to Puerto Rico. Among the landscapes it has preserved are parts of Alaska's Tongass National Forest — the world's largest coastal temperate rainforest — vast mountain ranges in central Idaho, and Appalachian forests in Virginia that protect municipal water supplies for more than 75,000 residents.

The rule has survived legal challenges before. Wyoming brought a lawsuit challenging it, and the George W. Bush administration attempted to replace the national rule with state-specific plans. Ultimately, the rule was upheld and reinstated in 2011.

Wildfire Debate at the Center

The administration's central argument for rescinding the rule rests on wildfire prevention. The U.S. is suffering one of its worst wildfire years on record, with 7.3 million acres burned in roughly 49,000 fires through August 17, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

"Opening our backcountry forests to more roads and development, and therefore more ignitions, is also not a wildfire solution, and never will be."

— Josh Hicks, Director of Conservation Campaigns, The Wilderness Society

Environmental groups counter that research published by the Forest Service itself during the first Trump administration showed that more wildfires ignite near roads, wildfire mitigation efforts have been more common in roadless areas, and roadless areas have no effect on wildfire burn rates. A 2025 analysis by the Wilderness Society found wildfire density is lowest in wilderness and protected areas.

"This would be the single largest evisceration of public lands protections in American history," said Randi Spivak, public lands policy director at the Center for Biological Diversity. "Roadless forests are the beating heart of biodiversity. Forest areas free of roads and logging provide crucial refuge and connected habitat for more than 500 imperiled species."

Industry Faces Its Own Headwinds

Even if the rule is rescinded, timber companies face practical barriers. The Forest Service has proposed slashing its budget by 63% in fiscal 2026, and at least 7,500 employees have reportedly already left the agency amid federal layoffs. The agency's existing 370,000-mile road network already carries a maintenance backlog in the billions.

"The USFS simply does not have the money to embark on a road-building bonanza to attempt to meet the administration's clearly arbitrary and aspirational timber targets," said Susan Jane Brown, principal attorney at Silvix Resources, an Oregon-based environmental law firm.

East of the Mississippi, there is little immediate demand for hardwood timber, with China — traditionally the biggest market — not buying from U.S. companies amid trade tensions. And some forest management plans already protect roadless areas independently of the federal rule.

What Comes Next

The rollback is expected to affect roughly 44 million acres, as Rollins confirmed in June that separate rules protecting about 13.5 million acres in Idaho and Colorado would remain in place. Environmental groups including Earthjustice are preparing for legal challenges but remain in a wait-and-see mode until the rulemaking advances further.

The agency will accept public comment on the proposed rule until September 21, with a full environmental analysis expected later this year and a final decision anticipated in the fall of 2026. Some 154 conservation groups have already called on Congress to permanently ban logging in the affected areas.
